doc.title: Gene Bertoncini interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001

title: Advice to young guitarists
summary: He advises learning standards, taking experience over pay, and following your heart, with a story of college friends.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: What would be your advice to guitar students in colleges these days to prepare themselves for what’s available now?

I think the most important thing is to develop your repertoire, learn as many tunes as possible. I think still the standard songs are still what gets you the gigs in life, if you can play. If they know you can play older tunes and if you can improvise and bend with situations and be a nice person. Above all just follow your heart and keep the faith. There is room for everybody in some fashion, as we can see at this convention. There are now seven thousand people here and there are seven thousand more musicians probably this

year looking for work. But everybody’s got a smile on their face. You know, try, and success has very little to do with money. It’s got a lot to do with your ability to play, and the chance to play. And I would say not to turn down anything because of a lack of — because it didn’t pay enough or something like that. Get as many experiences as you can to play. However, there are guys that try to always get you to play for nothing that shouldn’t do that either.
Don’t take that too far, yeah.

So there are people that can afford to pay a little more money to musicians but they always keep them on that servant level. And that’s a shame. But I think there is room for everybody. And follow your heart, follow your blisses, as Joseph Campbell said. And I just had breakfast, as I said, with my roommates, one of my roommates was a pianist in college. And he later went on to be, through the Marine Corps, a pilot for Delta Airlines. And he retired from Delta Airlines and he’s now a junior in college studying music. And he’s happier than he can ever be. And the other guy is studying bass. He headed the whole Wendy’s chain commercials. He did all those commercials. Those are such a nice bunch of commercials for Wendy’s. He was in charge of all that for years. And now he’s retired. Charlie Rath is his name. And we talked about that music — and they love me because I stayed with it. But I had this other special gift. But here we all are together, we just talk about music.
